name: Gas Distribution as Regulated Capital Compounding
deck: While electric utilities captured headlines on reliability and load growth, gas-distribution systems proved resilient through regulated capital compounding and rate-base growth. Atmos Energy and ONE Gas exemplify how natural-gas distribution remains economically viable despite energy-transition pressure. Both companies relied on rate relief, system-integrity capex, customer growth in constructive jurisdictions, and weather-normalization mechanisms to deliver EPS growth of 6-8% without commodity upside or volume acceleration. The sub-pattern shows that regulated gas infrastructure is not a sunset asset class; it is a steady capital-deployment machine where rate design and regulatory recovery matter more than gas demand growth.
core_bet: Regulated gas utilities that can sustain capital investment, achieve timely rate recovery, and operate in jurisdictions supporting customer growth will deliver reliable earnings and cash flow even as energy transition reduces long-term gas consumption. Rate lag reduction and infrastructure modernization are the key levers.

numbers.label: ONE Gas FY2025 capex and asset removal costs

mechanism: Atmos and ONE Gas operate under cost-of-service regulation in their respective service territories. Rate cases and regulatory adjustments govern earnings quality, not commodity pricing or volume growth. Both companies filed and won rate cases in FY2025-2026 that improved net margins and reduced regulatory lag.

Capital investment drives rate-base growth, which in turn drives allowed-return earnings. Atmos targets $26B capex through FY2030 to grow rate base from $21.4B to $42B. ONE Gas completed rate cases covering Oklahoma, Kansas, and Texas. Both companies described capex as 85%+ safety and reliability driven (pipe replacement, system integrity), which regulators favor and customers accept.

Weather normalization mechanisms protect earnings when conditions diverge from normal. ONE Gas Q1 2026 faced 20.5% warmer-than-normal and 24.6% warmer-than-prior-year weather, but weather-normalization mechanisms kept earnings resilient. This is a core feature that makes the model less cyclical than incumbent merchant generators or unregulated gas retailers.
why_now: The inflection was regulatory and customer-growth driven, not commodity driven. Atmos and ONE Gas each filed multi-year rate cases in 2024-2025 seeking approval for higher capital investment and service-territory expansion. Atmos highlighted $26B through FY2030 capex as modernization for an aging system serving 3.4M customers. ONE Gas emphasized customer growth in Oklahoma and Texas, where population and industrial migration supported line extensions and new connections. By Q2-Q3 2026, both companies had achieved rate relief (Atmos raised FY2026 EPS guidance midway through the year; ONE Gas raised FY2026 guidance to the upper half of prior ranges) and were describing momentum in customer additions and capital deployment. This was not a rebound from a trough; it was steady compounding of a stable business model as rates caught up to capital spend.
who_pays: Household and commercial gas users absorb steady rate increases tied to capital investment and inflation. Industrial customers may face higher feedstock costs if gas prices rise, but core consumers see steady bills rather than volatile swings.
who_profits: Shareholders of regulated gas utilities that operate in growing jurisdictions (Oklahoma, Texas) and have supportive regulators (Oklahoma Corporation Commission, Kansas Corporation Commission, Texas Railroad Commission). Contractors and suppliers winning capital-deployment contracts. Energy-efficiency businesses that can serve the same customer base.
tension: The tension is between rate increases (needed to fund capex and returns) and customer affordability pressure. As gas consumption declines due to electrification and efficiency, per-unit costs may rise even if absolute dollars remain stable. Regulators must balance investment incentives against affordability concerns.
surprising_part: ONE Gas Q1 2026 showed that earnings can improve even when weather is sharply warmer than normal and delivered volumes decline. Normalization mechanisms and rate relief overcame physical-demand weakness. This is a crucial inversion: regulated gas utilities can grow earnings while shrinking physical volumes if regulators allow rate increases and capital recovery. This flips the traditional commodity story where volume growth is the main driver.
one_sentence: Regulated gas distributors shifted from commodity exposure to capital-compounding models, using rate relief, infrastructure investment, and weather-normalization mechanisms to deliver steady EPS growth independent of gas demand.
societal_stake: Gas infrastructure modernization supports reliability and safety for millions of households and industrial customers. If investment falters due to regulatory lag or affordability pressure, aging systems degrade. If rates rise too steeply, lower-income households face energy affordability challenges.

evidence.fact: Fiscal Q3 2026 EPS $7.33 on net income $1.2B; fiscal Q2 2026 EPS $5.92; fiscal Q1 2026 EPS $2.44. Full-year guidance reaffirmed at $8.40-$8.50. YTD capex $3.1B (85%+ safety/reliability), rate base $21.4B growing toward $42B by FY2030, and guidance for 6-8% EPS and dividend growth through FY2030.

FY2025 net income $264.2M, diluted EPS $4.37, adjusted EPS $4.48. Q1 2026 (warmest quarter on record for service territory at 20.5% warmer than normal, 24.6% warmer than prior year) still delivered EPS $2.04, adjusted EPS $2.11, showing resilience despite 42% warm weather in Q2 2026. Full-year FY2025 capex $759.5M, with management emphasizing weather normalization and new rates as the main drivers of operating-income growth.
